notes.1a: Many candidates found this question accessible with the majority correctly identifying the conical flask and the gas syringe as the items of apparatus in the diagram. Candidates who performed less well incorrectly identified the gas syringe as a ruler or a measuring tube or measuring cylinder.
notes.1b: Candidates often did not refer to the information on the question regarding the temperature range required for fermentation. Many candidates simply said to ‘keep it at a constant temperature’ or ‘to maintain the temperature’. Stronger responses stated that the water bath is used to keep the mixture between 25C and 35C. Fermentation is exothermic and without cooling it can exceed 35C, but in a cool environment the temperature can cool to below 25C.
notes.1c: This was well answered with most candidates correctly stating that the volume of gas was still increasing or that it had not stopped making gas.
notes.1d: (i) Candidates found this question easy and most candidates could state the effect of carbon dioxide on limewater was for the limewater to turn cloudy. Candidates who performed well were able to state that the cloudiness observed was due to the formation of a white precipitate.
notes.1dii: This question proved to be more demanding. Stronger responses from candidates who performed well gave the expected answer that there would be no more bubbles (because no more gas would be made). Weaker responses stated that the limewater would stop turning cloudy or changing, but if it is already cloudy you cannot see if it stops turning cloudy.
notes.1e: While the majority of candidates correctly stated that distillation should be used, a significant number of candidates incorrectly stated filtration.
notes.2a: Candidates performed well on this question and the most gained full credit. The most common errors included incorrect readings from the diagrams and leaving times in minutes and seconds rather than converting to seconds only. Almost all candidates had recorded the times to the nearest whole number. It is generally not appropriate to quote reaction times in tenths or hundredths of a second for chemistry experiments due to factors like limitations in measurement precision.
notes.2b: Most of the graphs had a suitable scale on the y-axis, usually 2 cm grid square = 10 seconds. Some candidates selected difficult scales where each 2 cm grid square was 1.5 or 3; these candidates often made errors in plotting. Each large grid square should be 1, 2 or 5  10n. The points were generally correctly plotted. There were many who thought that lines of best fit must be straight lines. The curves of best fit were often poorly drawn. Straight sections on a curve of best fit, very thick lines or any double line where a gap is visible between the lines not acceptable.
notes.2c: (i) Candidates performed well on this question and were able to calculate the relative rate using the formula given. Candidates who did not evaluate the fraction gained no credit as there had been no attempt at a calculation.
notes.2cii: This was one of the most accessible questions on the paper and almost all candidates identified that experiment 1 had the greatest relative rate.
notes.2d: (i) Most candidates were able to calculate the volume of water and give the appropriate unit. Less well performing candidates found this question difficult, as they had not understood that the total volume of solution had to remain constant. They often gained credit for units even with an incorrect calculation. �PAGE�68
notes.2dii: Nearly all candidates could work out the relevant time for the text to not be visible at 37 cm3. To gain full credit working had to be shown as stated in the question. The clearest working is the use of construction lines. Candidates who performed less well chose the incorrect volume; the most common was using 36 or 38.5 cm3 rather than 37 cm3.
notes.2iii: Candidates performed poorly on this question and found it very challenging. Most candidates just restated ‘so that the total volume is kept constant’ or said ‘so that it is a fair test’. Few appreciated that if the total volume changes between experiments, you are introducing a second variable, which would make it unclear whether any changes in reaction rate are due to concentration or to volume.
notes.2e: (i) This was the most accessible question on the paper, with almost all candidates having an understanding that burettes measure volumes more accurately than measuring cylinders.
notes.2eii: This question was answered well. Candidates were able to state that either pipettes had fixed volumes or that the pipette sizes available were too small and could not hold the larger variable volumes of sodium thiosulfate required.
notes.2f: This was found to be the most challenging question on the paper and few correct answers were seen. Many candidates incorrectly related their answer to surface area and rate of reaction without realising that a beaker will have a larger cross section and so result in a shallower depth of liquid; this makes it easier to see through and so it takes more time for the text to be obscured.
notes.3a: As the question stated that NaOH should be added dropwise and then in excess, candidates should give an observation for each step. As solution L contained an aluminium salt, a white precipitate is formed on dropwise addition which should dissolve in excess.
notes.3b: Similarly, as the question stated that aqueous ammonia should be added dropwise and then in excess, candidates should give an observation for each step. As solution L contained an aluminium salt, a white precipitate is formed on dropwise addition which should remain excess. Candidates who made use of the notes for qualitative analysis on the last two pages of the question paper normally performed well on Questions 3(a) and 3(b).
notes.3c: Again, candidates who made use of the notes for qualitative analysis on the last two pages of the question paper normally stated correctly that a white precipitate would form as solution L contained chloride ions.
notes.3d: The test carried out was the test for sulfate ions. As solid L was a chloride there should have been no change. A common error was to say a white precipitate would form (the positive result in the sulfate test). It is important that the candidates use all the information given to them in the question.
notes.3e: This was an accessible question for candidates and most could identify the gas given off from the nitrate test as ammonia.
notes.3f: Candidates who performed well often gained full credit for the identification of solid M as barium nitrate. It was not uncommon for candidates to identify only that solid M contained barium ions and not include an anion in their answer. �PAGE�69
notes.4: This planning question was well answered with many candidates gaining full credit. Candidates made good use of the information provided. This was a task which involved the preparation of a pure, dry sample of solid lead(II) chloride. Most candidates used a method based on the information in the question. The expected steps in the plan were: • addition of water to solid lead(II) nitrate and addition of water to solid sodium chloride • stirring the mixtures so that both solids dissolved forming aqueous solutions • addition of both the aqueous solutions together • using a suitable container such as a beaker or boiling tube • filtration of the precipitate from the aqueous sodium nitrate • washing of the precipitate with water to remove aqueous sodium nitrate impurities • drying of the precipitate by leaving in a warm place. Many excellent and succinct answers were seen. However, a common reason for candidates not obtaining full credit was the omission of details. For example, some candidates did not specify stirring to aid dissolving or washing and drying the precipitate. Candidates who performed less well did not dissolve the solids at the start and began their method by adding the aqueous solutions together. A small number of candidates added the solids together so the precipitation reaction would not work. A significant minority confused the terms filtrate and residue. Some candidates choose unsuitable pieces of equipment for making their salt such as a burette, measuring cylinder, volumetric flask or trough. Suitable containers would include beakers, conical flasks, boiling tubes or test-tubes. A small number of candidates gained no credit for drying the precipitate as no method of drying was given. ‘Dry’ is not sufficient but ‘leave to dry in a warm place’ would gain credit. There is no need for candidates to write a list of aims and apparatus at the start of their answers. The aim of the plan is in the question and credit will not be given for listing items of apparatus; where credit is available for the selection of an appropriate item of apparatus then it must be clear in the plan for what the item of apparatus will be used. Writing a list of dependent, independent and control variables is also not necessary.
notes.key_messages:
• In the qualitative analysis question (Question 3), candidates were expected to use the term ‘precipitate’
when describing the formation of a solid from the reaction between two solutions. If when two solutions
are mixed the product becomes cloudy and opaque, then a precipitate has been formed.
• When a question asks for observations, then stating that a gas is given off is not an observation. The
relevant observation would be effervescence or fizzing or bubbles (of a gas). Similarly, when asked for
observations when a gas has been evolved, then identifying the gas is not an observation. The test and
the result of the test are needed.
• Not all the tests described will necessarily give a positive result; a negative test result is useful since it
tells us that a certain ion is not in the compound being tested.
• When a question asks for the name of a chemical, a correct formula is always acceptable. However, if a
candidate answers with an incorrect formula, then credit will not be awarded.
• When plotting graphs, points should be plotted as a cross (x) or an encircled dot () and not obscured
by the graph line, which should be drawn using a sharp pencil. A line of best fit can be curved or straight
– whichever is the best fit for the data points. Straight lines should be drawn with the aid of a rule and
not drawn freehand; curves should be smooth and not just a line which moves from point to point.
Graph scales should be chosen such that the plotted data takes up over half of the available space and
it is recommended that each major grid line should be equivalent to 1, 2, or 5 (or those numbers
multiplied by 10n) - this is indicated in the Presentation of Data section of the syllabus in the section
entitled ‘Graphs’ (and also recommended by the Association for Science Education (A.S.E.)).
• Readings recorded from a given item of apparatus should all be recorded to the same resolution (the
same number of decimal places).
notes.general_comments:
The vast majority of candidates successfully attempted all the questions and the full range of marks was
seen. Most candidates were able to complete the questions in the time available. The paper discriminated
successfully between candidates of different abilities but was accessible to all and was generally well-
answered, with very few blank spaces.
In answering the planning question (Question 4), there is no need for candidates to write a list of apparatus
at the start, nor the aims of the experiment, nor a list of safety precautions. Where there is credit available for
the use of suitable apparatus, this will only be awarded if it is stated what the apparatus is used for. This will
not be awarded just for a name in a list of other apparatus.
There evidence to suggest that more practical work was being used in the teaching of this syllabus than has
been seen in the last few years.
